category.title: Intervals & Sweep Line
category.description: Interval merging, insertions, intersections, meeting room scheduling, and sweep line event patterns.

algorithms.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
algorithms.summary: Sorts intervals by start time and greedily merges overlapping intervals into a minimal list of non-overlapping intervals.
explanation: 1. Sort input intervals in ascending order by their start time `interval[0]`.
2. Initialize `merged` list with the first interval.
3. Iterate through intervals. If current interval starts before or at previous interval's end (`curr[0] <= last[1]`), merge them by setting `last[1] = max(last[1], curr[1])`.
4. Otherwise, no overlap occurs. Append current interval to `merged`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Merge Intervals on [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]]
traceSteps: Inspect [2, 6]: 2 <= 3 → Overlap! Extend end to max(3, 6) = 6. Active becomes [1, 6].
Inspect [8, 10]: 8 > 6 → No overlap. Push [1, 6]. Active becomes [8, 10].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines overlapping time intervals into disjoint contiguous blocks.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when consolidating schedule availability or overlapping physical memory ranges.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Calendar applications, memory allocators, audio segment merging.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorting by start time ensures single-pass linear O(N) overlap merging.

algorithms.title: Insert Interval into Sorted Non-Overlapping List
algorithms.summary: Inserts a new interval into a pre-sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and merges any overlapping intervals in O(N) time.
explanation: 1. Phase 1 (Pre-overlap): Add all intervals that end before `newInterval` starts (`interval[1] < newInterval[0]`).

2. Phase 2 (Overlap Merge): While intervals overlap with `newInterval` (`interval[0] <= newInterval[1]`), merge them into `newInterval` by setting `newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], interval[0])` and `newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], interval[1])`.
3. Append merged `newInterval` to output.
4. Phase 3 (Post-overlap): Add all remaining intervals after `newInterval`.

exampleTrace.title: Trace Insert newInterval=[2,5] into [[1,3], [6,9]]
traceSteps: Inspect [1, 3]: Overlaps with [2, 5] (1 <= 5). Merge → newInterval becomes [min(1,2), max(3,5)] = [1, 5].
Inspect [6, 9]: Starts at 6 > 5 (after newInterval). Append merged [1, 5], then append [6, 9].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Inserts a new event into an existing conflict-free schedule in O(N) time without full array re-sorting.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when inserting new events into an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Real-time calendar event creation, stream-based interval maintenance.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Leverages existing sorted order to complete insertion and merging in a single O(N) pass.

codeTemplates.code:
def insert(intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    res = []
    i = 0
    n = len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]:
        newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0])
        newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    res.append(newInterval)
    while i < n:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    return res

algorithms.title: Interval List Intersections
algorithms.summary: Finds the intersection of two sorted lists of closed intervals using a Two-Pointer traversal.
explanation: 1. Maintain pointers `i` for `firstList` and `j` for `secondList`.
2. Calculate overlap bounds: `start = max(firstList[i][0], secondList[j][0])` and `end = min(firstList[i][1], secondList[j][1])`.
3. If `start <= end`, a valid intersection `[start, end]` exists. Append to output.
4. Advance pointer corresponding to the interval that ends first: if `firstList[i][1] < secondList[j][1]`, increment `i`, else increment `j`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes exact overlapping time windows between two independent availability lists.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when finding common available meeting times between two users' calendars.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Calendar meeting schedulers (Google Meet find a time), signal frequency overlap detection.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Two-pointer approach computes intersections in linear time O(N + M) without nested loops.

algorithms.title: Non-overlapping Intervals (Erase Overlaps)
algorithms.summary: Finds the minimum number of intervals to remove to make the remaining intervals non-overlapping using Greedy choice.
explanation: 1. Greedy Strategy: Sort intervals by end time `interval[1]` in ascending order.
2. Always keep the interval that finishes earliest. This leaves maximum room for future intervals.
3. Maintain `prevEnd = -inf`. For each interval `[start, end]`:
- If `start >= prevEnd`, no overlap! Keep interval and update `prevEnd = end`.
- Else, overlap detected! Remove this interval (increment `removeCount`).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines minimum deletions required to remove all conflicting time intervals.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when scheduling maximum number of compatible jobs on a single machine.
wAnswers.whereUsed: CPU single-core job schedulers, television show Recording planners.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorting by end time greedily minimizes future resource blockage.

algorithms.title: Meeting Rooms I (Can Attend All Meetings)
algorithms.summary: Determines if a single person can attend all scheduled meeting intervals without any overlap.
explanation: 1. Sort meeting intervals by their start time `interval[0]`.
2. Iterate through meetings from index 1 to N-1.
3. If current meeting starts before previous meeting ends (`curr[0] < prev[1]`), a schedule conflict occurs! Return `False`.
4. If no conflicts are found across all meetings, return `True`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Validates single-user schedule feasibility without time collisions.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when verifying if a single resource can accommodate all requested time slots.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Doctor appointment checkers, room reservation validation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorting by start time allows simple pairwise adjacent comparison in O(N) linear scan.

algorithms.title: Meeting Rooms II (Min Conference Rooms)
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(N) for start/end time arrays or min-heap
algorithms.summary: Calculates the minimum number of conference rooms required to accommodate all meetings using Min-Heap or Two Pointers.
explanation: 1. Extract and sort `start` times and `end` times independently.
2. Maintain `startPtr` and `endPtr`.
3. If `start[startPtr] < end[endPtr]`, a meeting starts before the earliest ending meeting finishes → Room count +1!
4. Otherwise, a room freed up! Advance `endPtr`.
5. The peak rooms required simultaneously across the timeline is the answer.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes peak concurrency / minimum physical rooms required to hold overlapping events.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when determining maximum overlapping intervals at any given moment.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Conference center room manager, server instance autoscalers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Separate sorting of start and end times yields optimal O(N log N) sweep computation.

algorithms.title: Minimum Railway Platforms Required
algorithms.summary: Calculates the minimum number of railway platforms required for a station to avoid train collisions.
explanation: 1. Extract arrival times `arr` and departure times `dep` into separate arrays.
2. Sort both `arr` and `dep` in ascending order.
3. Use Two Pointers `i` (arrival) and `j` (departure). Maintain `count` of currently occupied platforms and `maxPlatforms`.
4. If `arr[i] <= dep[j]`, train arrives before previous train leaves → increment `count` and `i`.
5. Else, train departs → decrement `count` and increment `j`.

traceSteps: arr=940 > dep=910 → Train 1 left! count=0, depPtr=1.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines maximum simultaneous train occupancy at a transit station.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when determining capacity requirements for concurrent arrival/departure events.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Railway dispatch systems, airport gate scheduling, bus terminal management.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Separate array sorting enables two-pointer linear sweep in O(N log N) time.

codeTemplates.code:
def findPlatform(arr: list[int], dep: list[int]) -> int:
    arr.sort()
    dep.sort()
    i = j = 0
    count = max_platforms = 0
    n = len(arr)
    while i < n and j < n:
        if arr[i] <= dep[j]:
            count += 1
            max_platforms = max(max_platforms, count)
            i += 1
        else:
            count -= 1
            j += 1
    return max_platforms

algorithms.title: Sweep Line Algorithm (Events & Skyline Pattern)
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log N) for event sorting and Priority Queue
algorithms.summary: Transforms interval start/end boundaries into discrete events and sweeps across the timeline to maintain dynamic active state.
explanation: 1. Event Transformation: Convert each interval `[start, end, val]` into two point events: Start Event `(start, +val)` and End Event `(end, -val)`.
2. Event Sorting: Sort all events by timestamp. Tie-breaking: process start events before end events if boundaries coincide.
3. Sweep Line Execution: Iterate through sorted events. Maintain running active capacity / height using a Hash Map or Max-PriorityQueue.
4. Record skyline key points, peak capacity, or overlap thresholds as sweep line moves forward.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes dynamic continuous timeline states over geometric and temporal interval events.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for Skyline problem, Car Pooling capacity, My Calendar III, and 2D rectangle intersections.
wAnswers.whereUsed: GIS spatial layout engines, building skyline renderers, dynamic ride-sharing capacity checks.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Converting 2D/range operations into 1D sorted event sweeps reduces complexity to O(N log N).
